paragraphs: Common name: Chinese Fan Palm / Fountain PalmThe earlier research also mentions Coconut palm tree, but the more detailed identification points to Chinese Fan Palm.
Scientific name: Livistona chinensis (Jacq.) R.Br. ex Mart.Family: Arecaceae — the palm family.
Characteristics for identification:
The leaves are large and fan-shaped.
The technical term for this type of leaf is palmate or costapalmate.
Many narrow leaf segments spread out from one central point.
The tips of the segments hang down, which gives the plant its fountain-like look.
The leaves are glossy green.
As the plant grows, it develops a slender upright trunk.
The leaf stalks can be quite long and may have small spines, especially when the plant is young.
Uses:It is mainly used as an ornamental plant in gardens, parks, avenues and landscaped areas.
Origin:The detailed research identifies it as the Chinese Fan Palm, native to China and nearby parts of East Asia rather than India.
Flowering and fruits:The research notes flowering around January–February in some Indian records, but this can change depending on climate and location.
After flowering, it produces small rounded fruits. They start green and can become blue-green to dark purple or almost black as they mature.
Growth:It is considered a relatively slow-growing palm.
Interesting fact:The word “palmate” comes from the Latin word palma, meaning the palm of the hand. The leaf looks a little like the fingers of a hand spreading out from one point.
Common name: Guava / Guava tree
Scientific name: Psidium guajava L.Family: Myrtaceae.
Characteristics for identification:
It is usually a small tree or large shrub.
The leaves are oval to oblong and have very visible veins.
The bark can look smooth and pale brown or copper-coloured.
The flowers are white and usually occur singly or in small groups.
The fruit is round or oval and can have green or yellowish skin when mature.

Origin:Guava is originally from tropical America. The detailed research describes it as especially associated with Mexico and Central and South America. It is now grown in many tropical and subtropical countries, including India. A3 Project Details (2)(1)
Uses:This is mainly a fruit tree. Guava is eaten fresh and is also used in juices, jams, jellies and other food products. It is an important cultivated fruit crop in India.

Flowers and flowering season:The flowers are small, white and usually grow in the leaf axils. Guava does not have just one fixed flowering season everywhere. In India, different crop cycles can produce flowering around February–March, June–July or October–November, depending on the region and cultivation method.
Interesting fact:Guava is well known for its nutritional value and is a good source of vitamin C.

Medicinal/nutritional note:Guava has been used traditionally for different purposes, and the fruit is nutritious. However, traditional medicinal use should not be presented as proof that guava cures a disease. Kew records food and medicinal uses for the species. Plants of the World Online
False Ashoka / False Ashok / Mast tree
Common name: False Ashoka / False Ashok / Mast Tree
Scientific name: Polyalthia longifolia (Sonn.) Thwaites
Characteristics for identification:
It is a tall, narrow evergreen tree.
The leaves are long, narrow and lance-shaped.
They can be around 15–25 cm long.
The edges of the leaves are noticeably wavy.
The branches are slender and tend to droop.
The tree often has a tall, elegant shape.
Origin:It is native to southern India and Sri Lanka and is now widely planted throughout India and other tropical regions.

Uses:It is mainly planted as an ornamental tree, especially along roads, around schools and institutions, and in gardens. Its narrow shape makes it useful where a tall tree is wanted without taking up too much sideways space.
Flowers:The flowers are much less noticeable than the leaves. They are:
small
greenish-yellow
star-like
found along the branches or near the leaf axils.
The tree also produces small clustered fruits that become darker as they mature. A

Medicinal/traditional use:The bark has traditionally been used as a febrifuge, meaning something used traditionally to reduce fever. Research has also looked at extracts of the bark and leaves for antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory and other possible effects. These are traditional or laboratory findings, not proven treatments.
Important fact:Despite its common name, False Ashoka is not the true Ashoka tree. The true Ashoka is Saraca asoca. These two plants should not be confused.
Common name: Coral Plant / Coral Bush / Physic Nut
Scientific name: Jatropha multifida L.Family: Euphorbiaceae.
Characteristics for identification:
It is a shrub or small tree.
Its leaves are very distinctive because they are deeply divided into many narrow lobes.
The leaf can look almost like a hand with many thin fingers.
The leaves have long stalks.
It produces bright coral-red flowers in clusters on long stalks.
The fruit is roughly three-sided and becomes yellowish when mature.
Origin:It is native to tropical and subtropical America, especially Mexico and the Caribbean, and has been introduced into many tropical regions including India. Plants of the World Online
Uses:In India it is mainly grown as an ornamental garden plant and can be seen in gardens, parks and landscaped campuses.
Flowering season:India Flora Online records flowering and fruiting roughly from August to May, although the exact timing can vary with climate. India Flora
Fruit:The fruit is about 2.5–3 cm and has three angles. It becomes yellowish when mature and usually contains three seeds. A3 Project Details
Medicinal/traditional uses:Traditional uses include applying latex to wounds, using leaves for scabies and other traditional preparations.

Important warning:This is one plant where the safety information is important. The fruits and seeds can be poisonous if eaten. Reported effects of poisoning include vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps and weakness. It should not be used as a home remedy without proper medical guidance.
Common name: Frangipani / Singapore Frangipani / White Frangipani / Temple Flower
Scientific name: Plumeria obtusa L.
Characteristics for identification:
It is a shrub or small tree.
The leaves are thick and green.
The leaves are generally broad, smooth and rounded or slightly notched at the tip.
The flowers are white with a yellow centre.
The flowers have about five petals and have a waxy appearance.
The flowers are usually strongly fragrant.
Flowers:The flowers are one of the main reasons this plant is grown. They are used for:
religious offerings
garlands
decoration
perfumes and fragrances
Origin:Plumeria obtusa is native to parts of Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean and is now grown in many tropical regions. Plants of the World Online
Fruit:After flowering, it can produce paired, long seed pods. When the pods mature, they split open and release many winged seeds. The wings help the seeds move through the air.

Medicinal/traditional uses:Traditional uses have been reported for wounds, some skin conditions and other purposes. These uses should be treated as traditional or experimental, not as proven medical treatments.
Safety:The plant produces a milky latex or sap that can irritate the skin and is considered poisonous.
Fun fact:Frangipani is especially famous for its beautiful, fragrant flowers, which is why it is so common around temples and gardens.
Common name: Peacock Flower / Barbados Pride / Dwarf Poinciana
Scientific name: Caesalpinia pulcherrima (L.) Sw.Family: Fabaceae.
Characteristics for identification:
It is usually a shrub or small tree.
The leaves are bipinnately compound, meaning the leaves are divided twice into many small leaflets.
The flowers are very bright and can be red, orange, yellow or a mixture of these colours.
The flowers have very long stamens sticking out beyond the petals.
The stems can have small prickles.
It produces flat, elongated seed pods. Plants of the World Online
Origin:It is native to tropical America, especially areas from southeastern Mexico to Central America. It is now widely grown in India and other tropical countries. Plants of the World Online
Uses:It is mainly grown as an ornamental plant because of its bright flowers. It is used in gardens, along roadsides, hedges and landscaped areas.

Flowering season:Indian botanical records report flowering and fruiting throughout the year, while some regional sources give periods such as May–October. So it is better to say that it can flower for a long period in warm climates. India Flora
Fruit:It produces flat, elongated pods which become darker as they mature and contain several seeds.
Interesting fact:The long stamens sticking out from the flowers are one of the reasons the flower looks so unusual and showy.

Medicinal note:Different parts of the plant have traditional medicinal uses, but some preparations can also be harmful. For the project, it is better to describe these as traditional uses rather than proven treatments. Plants of the World Online
Common name: Madagascar Periwinkle / Sadabahar / Sadaphuli
Scientific name: Catharanthus roseus (L.) G.DonFamily: Apocynaceae.
Characteristics for identification:
It is a small, bushy herb or subshrub.
The leaves are dark green, glossy and arranged opposite each other.
The flowers have five broad petals.
Flowers can be white, pink or purple.
The plant contains a milky sap.
Origin:It is native to Madagascar, not India. It is now grown widely in tropical and subtropical countries, including India. A3 Project Details (2)(1)

Flowers and flowering season:The flowers are small but very noticeable. In warm climates, the plant can flower almost throughout the year rather than having one short flowering season. A3 Project Details (2)(1)
Fruit:Instead of a fleshy fruit, it produces two narrow seed pods, called follicles. They contain many dark seeds.
Uses:It is commonly grown as an ornamental garden plant.

Medicinal importance:This plant has a very interesting connection with medicine. Scientists discovered compounds in it that helped lead to the development of vincristine and vinblastine, medicines used in cancer treatment.
Important warning:The plant also contains powerful natural chemicals and should not be eaten or used as a home remedy. Its sap is toxic.
Fun fact:The same small garden plant that looks simple and pretty has contributed to important medicines used to treat cancer.
Common name: Drumstick Tree / Moringa / Munga / Shevga
Scientific name: Moringa oleifera Lam.Family: Moringaceae.
Characteristics for identification:
The leaves look very fine and feathery.
What looks like many tiny leaves is actually one large compound leaf divided many times.
The flowers are small, pale white or creamy-white and fragrant.
The tree usually has a slender trunk and an open crown.
Its famous long hanging pods look like drumsticks.
Origin:Moringa is actually native to the Indian subcontinent, unlike many of the ornamental plants in the garden. It is now grown throughout tropical regions.

Flowers and flowering season:The flowers are fragrant and occur in loose clusters. Flowering varies by region. It can flower several times a year in warm climates, and some Indian regions have major flowering around February–March.
Uses:Almost the whole plant has uses.
Young pods are eaten as vegetables.
Leaves are eaten as vegetables.
Flowers can also be eaten.
Seeds contain oil.
The plant is widely used as a food crop.

Interesting fact:Moringa seeds have been studied for their ability to help clarify dirty water by making suspended particles clump together. However, this does not mean the treated water is automatically safe to drink; proper treatment is still needed.
Growth:Moringa is known for being fast-growing and can do well in warm and relatively dry conditions.
Medicinal note:Moringa is very nutritious, but many internet claims call it a “miracle tree.” It is better not to say that it cures diseases.
Common name: Oleander / Kaner / Karavira
Scientific name: Nerium oleander L.Family: Apocynaceae.
Characteristics for identification:
It is an evergreen shrub or small tree.
The leaves are long, narrow and pointed.
They are thick and leathery.
Leaves usually occur opposite each other or in groups.
The central vein of the leaf is quite noticeable.
Flowers grow in clusters near the ends of branches.
Origin:Oleander has a broad native range extending from the Mediterranean region through parts of the Middle East and Indian subcontinent to Myanmar. It is now grown widely in warm regions.
Uses:It is mainly used as an ornamental plant. It is popular because it can tolerate heat, drought, poor soil and some urban conditions. This is why it is often seen along roads and in gardens.
Flowers:Flowers can be pink, white, red or purple and usually have five spreading lobes.
Flowering season:It can have a long flowering period, especially in warm climates, and may produce flowers for much of the year.
Fruit:Instead of a fleshy fruit, it produces long narrow pods. When they open, they release seeds with fine hairs that help them move through the air.

Very important safety point:Every part of Oleander is highly poisonous if eaten. It contains cardiac glycosides such as oleandrin, which can affect the heart. Its sap can also irritate the skin, and burning the plant can produce harmful smoke.
Fun fact:Although it is poisonous to humans, Oleander is a food plant for the caterpillars of the Common Crow butterfly.
Common name: Taro / Elephant Ear / Arbi / Dasheen
Scientific name: Colocasia esculenta (L.) SchottFamily: Araceae.
Characteristics for identification:
Very large leaves.
Leaves are broadly heart-shaped or arrow-shaped.
The veins are very noticeable.
The leaf stalks are long and thick.
Several leaves grow together from the base.
The leaf stalk attaches toward the underside of the leaf rather than simply at the edge. This is called a peltate arrangement.
Origin:Its native range extends from India through southern China and Southeast Asia to Sumatra. It has been cultivated and spread to many tropical regions.
Uses:Taro is much more than an ornamental plant. It is an important food crop.
The underground part is a swollen storage stem called a corm. This is what we commonly eat as arbi or taro.
Young leaves and leaf stalks are also eaten in some cultures.
Flowers:The flowers are not very noticeable. Like other members of the Araceae family, it has a spadix surrounded by a spathe.
Flowering season:There is no single reliable flowering season. Some cultivated varieties may flower rarely.
Interesting fact:The huge leaves can shed water. Water droplets can sit on the surface and roll away instead of immediately soaking into the leaf.
Important safety point:Raw taro contains calcium oxalate crystals, which can cause burning and irritation in the mouth and throat. The edible parts need to be properly cooked.
Common name: Pomegranate / Anar
Scientific name: Punica granatum L.Family: Lythraceae.
Characteristics for identification:
It is a small tree or large, highly branched shrub.
The leaves are small, narrow and glossy.
Some branches may have short spines.
The fruits are round and reddish-brown when mature.
The most useful feature is the little crown at the top of the fruit.
Origin:Pomegranate is native to parts of Southwest and Central Asia, including areas around Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan. It has been cultivated widely in India.
Flowers:The flowers are usually bright red to orange-red and can be around 3–5 cm across.
Flowering season:Pomegranate does not have one fixed flowering season. In India, farmers can manage the flowering and fruiting cycles, so it can have more than one flowering period in a year.
Fruit and uses:The fruit is mainly eaten fresh. It is also used for:
juice
syrups
sauces
preserves
flavouring.
Inside the fruit are many seeds surrounded by juicy red or pink coverings called arils.
Best fun fact:The little “crown” on top of a pomegranate is actually part of the original flower. It is the flower's calyx, which remains attached as the fruit develops.
History:Pomegranate has been cultivated by humans for thousands of years.
Common name: Rose / Garden Rose
Scientific name: Rosa spp.Family: Rosaceae.
The exact species or variety cannot be confirmed from the photograph, because there are thousands of cultivated roses. So Rosa spp. is the safer scientific identification.
Characteristics for identification:
Woody, branching shrub.
Compound leaves made of several smaller leaflets.
Leaflets have serrated edges.
Stems have sharp structures called prickles.
Large, colourful flowers.
Bushy growth.
Important terminology:People usually call the sharp structures on roses “thorns,” but botanically they are more accurately called prickles. True thorns are different structures.
Flowers:Roses can be red, pink, white, yellow, orange, purple and many other shades. Some have only a few petals, while cultivated double roses can have many layers of petals.
Flowering season:There isn't one fixed season. Many modern garden roses can flower repeatedly, depending on the variety, climate and pruning.
Uses:Roses are grown for:
gardens
landscaping
bouquets
perfumes
decoration
cultural and ceremonial purposes.
Interesting fact:Roses produce a fruit-like structure called a rose hip after flowering. The rose hip contains the actual small fruits called achenes.
Another interesting fact:Many modern garden roses are the result of centuries of breeding and hybridization. So the roses we see in gardens are often very different from wild roses.
Common name: Golden Dewdrop / Sky Flower / Pigeon Berry
Scientific name: Duranta erecta L.Family: Verbenaceae — the verbena family.
Characteristics for identification:
Dense, branching shrub.
Small, smooth, oval to elliptical leaves.
Leaves are arranged opposite each other.
Some plants have spines on their branches.
The plant produces clusters of yellow-orange fruits.
Very important identification point:The bright yellow clusters seen in the photograph are fruits, not flowers.
The actual flowers of Duranta are usually blue, violet, lavender or sometimes white. The yellow-orange fruits appear later after flowering. A3 Project Details (2)(1)
Origin:It is native to tropical and subtropical America, but is now widely cultivated in warm regions including India.
Uses:It is mainly used for:
hedges
boundaries
screening
gardens
landscaping
topiary.
It can be pruned into different shapes.
Flowers and flowering season:The flowers are small and tubular and grow in long clusters. In warm climates, flowering can continue for a long period.
Fruit:The fruits are round, shiny and yellow to orange-yellow. They hang in clusters and are technically drupes, although the plant is commonly called Pigeon Berry.
Important safety point:The fruits should not be eaten by humans because they are considered poisonous. Birds can eat them and help spread the seeds.
Fun fact:This plant gives us a nice flower → fruit story: blue/violet flowers first, then yellow-orange fruits later.
Common name: Neem / Indian Neem / Margosa / Indian Lilac
Scientific name: Azadirachta indica A.Juss.Family: Meliaceae.
Characteristics for identification:
Medium to large evergreen tree.
Long pinnate compound leaves.
Each leaf is actually made up of many smaller leaflets.
Leaflets are narrow, pointed and have clearly serrated edges.
The tree develops a spreading crown.
Origin:Neem is native to South and Southeast Asia and is now grown widely in tropical regions. It is especially well suited to warm and relatively dry conditions.
Flowers:Neem produces small white, fragrant flowers in branching clusters.
Flowering season:In many parts of India, neem flowers around February–April, although the exact timing can vary with location. Fruits commonly appear later, around June–August in some regions.
Fruit:The fruit is a small oval or oblong drupe. It is green when young and becomes yellow or yellow-green when mature.
Uses:Almost every part of the neem tree has traditional uses. Some important ones are:
neem oil from the seeds
traditional datun from small twigs
shade and landscaping
wood for various products
agricultural pest control.

Very interesting fact:Neem seeds contain a compound called azadirachtin, which can interfere with the feeding, growth and reproduction of certain insect pests. This is why neem products are used in natural pest management.
Medicinal note:Neem has a long history in traditional medicine, but it is better not to say that neem simply “cures” diseases. Many medicinal claims still need stronger evidence.
Fun fact:Before modern toothbrushes became common, neem twigs were traditionally used as natural toothbrushes, called datun.
Common name: Chestnutleaf Trumpetbush / Yellow Trumpetbush
Scientific name: Tecoma castanifolia (D.Don) Melch.Family: Bignoniaceae — the trumpet-vine family.
Identification:The identification is considered probable rather than 100% certain, because Tecoma stans looks very similar. The main difference is in the leaves.
Characteristics for identification:
Leaves are usually simple, meaning one continuous leaf blade.
Leaves are long and lance-shaped.
They have strongly serrated edges.
Leaves are arranged opposite each other.
Flowers are bright golden-yellow and trumpet-shaped.
Flowers occur in clusters at the ends of branches.
The simple leaves are especially useful for separating it from Tecoma stans, which normally has several separate leaflets.
Origin:It is native to western South America, including areas of Ecuador and Peru. It is grown in India as an ornamental plant.
Flowers:The flowers are bright yellow and shaped like little trumpets. A large group in the photograph is actually made up of many individual flowers, not one giant flower.
Flowering season:In warm climates, it can have a long flowering period, but there isn't one reliable month that applies everywhere.
Fruit:After flowering it produces long, narrow seed capsules. When mature, the capsules split open and release seeds.
Uses:Mainly used as an ornamental plant in gardens, parks, borders and landscaped areas.
Fun fact:The name “Trumpetbush” makes sense because the flowers really do look like small yellow trumpets.
Common name: Indian Almond / Tropical Almond / Country Almond / Desi Badam / Jangli Badam
Scientific name: Terminalia catappa L.Family: Combretaceae.
Characteristics for identification:
Large, thick, glossy leaves.
Leaves are broadly oval or obovate.
Many leaves are grouped near the ends of branches.
Older trees can have branches growing in horizontal levels or tiers.
This can give the tree a layered or pagoda-like shape.
Leaves:One of the most interesting features is that older leaves can change colour before falling. They can become yellow, orange, red or even reddish-purple.
Flowers:The flowers are small and not very showy. They are white to greenish-white and occur in long slender spikes.
Flowering season:The exact timing varies by region, but Indian records give flowering during warmer months, roughly February–June in some areas.
Fruit:It produces a large, flattened, almond-shaped fruit. The fruit changes colour as it matures and contains a hard shell with an edible kernel.

Important distinction:Even though it is called Indian Almond, it is not the same plant as the true almond. Indian Almond is Terminalia catappa, while the true almond is Prunus dulcis. They belong to different plant families.
Uses:It is used as a shade and ornamental tree. The kernel can be eaten, and the wood has also been used for various purposes.
Fun fact:The fruit can float in water. This allows it to travel to other places and helps the seeds spread, especially in tropical coastal areas.
Common name: Yellow Bells / Yellow Trumpetbush
Scientific name: Tecoma stans (L.) Juss. ex KunthFamily: Bignoniaceae.
Characteristics for identification:
It has compound leaves.
Each leaf is divided into several separate leaflets.
Usually there are around 5–7 leaflets.
The leaflets are pointed and sharply serrated.
The flowers are bright yellow and trumpet-shaped.
Flowers appear in clusters near the ends of branches.
Important difference from Plant 15:Plant 15, Tecoma castanifolia, usually has simple leaves.
Plant 17, Tecoma stans, has compound leaves with several leaflets.
This is one of the best ways to tell the two apart when the yellow flowers look almost the same.
Origin:It is native to tropical and subtropical America, including Mexico, Central and South America and parts of the Caribbean. It has been introduced and cultivated in India.
Flowers and flowering season:The flowers are bright yellow, trumpet-shaped and around 4–5 cm long. In warm climates, it can flower for much of the year.
Fruit:After flowering, it produces a long, narrow seed capsule, sometimes around 10–20 cm long. When the capsule opens, it releases many seeds.
Fun fact:The seeds have thin, papery wings. These wings help the seeds move through the air, so the plant has its own simple way of spreading its seeds.
Uses:It is mainly planted for its bright flowers in:
gardens
parks
landscaping
borders
hedges.

Medicinal note:There are traditional and research claims about medicinal uses of Tecoma stans, but the research document specifically recommends not presenting it as a proven treatment for diseases. The flower, leaves and seed-dispersal facts are much safer and more useful for the school project.
Common name: Red-leaved Mussaenda / Ashanti Blood / Red Flag Bush
Scientific name: Mussaenda erythrophylla
Family: Rubiaceae
Characteristics
Shrubby growth.
Green leaves with prominent veins.
Small flowers occur in clusters.
Large bright-red, leaf-like structures surround the small flowers.
The most interesting part
The big red structures that look like petals are not actually the flower petals.
They are modified parts of the calyx, called enlarged sepals.
The actual flowers are much smaller and sit in the centre. They are usually pale or cream-white and star-shaped.
Flowering season
Generally spring to summer, although flowering can continue longer in warm tropical climates.
Uses
It is mainly an ornamental plant used in gardens, parks, borders and landscaped areas.
Fruit
It can produce small fleshy fruits or berries, but the fruit is not the main feature.
Medicinal use
Some Mussaenda species have traditional medicinal uses, but I would not make specific medicinal claims for M. erythrophylla without stronger evidence.
Interesting fact
The name “Ashanti Blood” comes from the striking blood-red colour of the enlarged floral structures.
The best student-friendly fact is:
“The part that catches your eye first isn't actually the flower!”
Common name: Purple Heart / Purple Queen
Scientific name: Tradescantia pallidaOften cultivated as Tradescantia pallida 'Purpurea'
Family: Commelinaceae
Characteristics for identification
Long, narrow, pointed leaves.
Leaves are deep purple or violet.
Stems are also purple and somewhat fleshy.
It usually grows low and spreads or trails along the ground.
The purple colour becomes stronger when the plant gets plenty of sunlight.
Flowers
The flowers are small compared with the leaves. They are usually pink to pale purple, with three petals and yellow stamens.
An individual flower lasts for only about one day, although the plant can keep producing new flowers.
Flowering season
It is mainly associated with warm weather and summer, but in suitable climates it can flower for much of the year.
Uses
It is mostly used as an ornamental plant for:
ground cover
garden borders
containers
hanging baskets
landscaping
It also grows quite easily from stem cuttings.
Medicinal benefits / harm
There are various medicinal claims about this plant, but the research does not support putting strong medicinal claims into the project.
Its sap can irritate the skin, and eating it may cause irritation in the mouth and stomach.
Interesting facts
One nice thing about this plant is that sunlight can make its purple colour stronger.
Another is that a small piece of stem can grow into a new plant.
Common name: Umbrella Tree / Octopus Tree
Scientific name: Heptapleurum actinophyllum
Older scientific name: Schefflera actinophylla
Family: Araliaceae
Characteristics for identification
An evergreen tree or large shrub.
It can have several trunks.
Its leaves are made up of several glossy leaflets.
The leaflets spread out from one point, almost like the spokes of an umbrella.
Mature leaves usually have several leaflets, often around 7–16.
Flowers
The flowers are small and red, but they grow in long clusters that spread outward from the top of the tree.
These clusters look a little like the arms of an octopus, which explains the name Octopus Tree.
Flowering season
In warm climates, flowering is generally associated with summer and can continue for several months. The exact timing depends on climate.
Fruit
After flowering, small round fruits develop. They can change from reddish colours to dark purple or blackish as they mature. Birds can eat them and help spread the seeds.
Origin and uses
It is native to northern Australia and New Guinea and is now widely grown in tropical and subtropical regions.
It is mainly used as an ornamental tree in gardens, parks and landscaped areas.
Interesting facts
It has two common names based on two different parts of the plant:
Umbrella Tree — because of the leaf shape.
Octopus Tree — because of the red flower clusters.
Another interesting fact is that in its natural rainforest habitat, it can sometimes begin growing on another tree and later send roots down to the ground.
Common name: Wild Plumeria / Bridal Bouquet / White Frangipani / Fiddle-leaf Plumeria
Scientific name: Plumeria pudica Jacq.
Family: Apocynaceae
Characteristics for identification
The leaves are the biggest clue.
Dark green and glossy.
Unusually broad toward the end.
They can look like little spoons or fiddles.
Flowers are white with small yellow centres.
Flowers occur in large clusters.
Flowers
The flowers have five white petals and a yellow centre. They grow in clusters that can look almost like a bouquet.
Unlike many other Frangipani plants, the flowers usually have little or no fragrance.
Flowering season
In warm climates, it can produce flowers for most of the year.
Fruit
It can produce paired, elongated seed pods after flowering, although the flowers and leaves are much more useful for identifying it.
Uses
It is mainly an ornamental plant and is used in:
gardens
parks
borders
walkways
containers
landscaped areas
Medicinal benefits / caution
There are traditional medicinal uses reported, but I would not make strong medical claims. Like other Plumeria, it produces milky sap, which can irritate the skin and eyes.
Interesting facts
The leaves look like spoons, which is one of the easiest ways to recognize this plant.
Also, the large clusters of white flowers look like a bridal bouquet, which explains one of its common names.
I think it is yellow bell
Common name: Yellow Double Hibiscus / Yellow Hibiscus / Gudhal / Jaba
Scientific name: Hibiscus rosa-sinensis cultivar
Family: Malvaceae
This is not a separate species. It is a cultivated form of Hibiscus rosa-sinensis.
Characteristics for identification
Large bright-yellow flowers.
Many layers of petals.
The flower looks full and ruffled.
Glossy green leaves.
Woody, branching shrub.
The double flower is the strongest clue.
Flowers and flowering season
Tropical hibiscus can flower repeatedly throughout the year in warm climates.
A flower generally opens during the day and closes later, although this can vary with the variety and conditions.
Uses
It is mainly an ornamental plant used in:
gardens
school gardens
parks
hedges
borders
pots and terraces
Hibiscus flowers are also culturally important in India and are often used in religious offerings.
Medicinal aspect
Hibiscus has a long history of traditional uses, but I would not say that this particular yellow ornamental variety cures anything.
Interesting fact
The word “double” does not mean the flower is twice as big. It means that the flower has extra layers of petals, making it look fuller.
Common name: White Frangipani / Singapore Frangipani / Frangipani
Scientific name: Plumeria obtusa L.
Family: Apocynaceae
Characteristics for identification
Thick, glossy, dark-green leaves.
Leaves are broad and elongated.
Leaf tips are rounded or blunt.
White flowers with five petals.
Yellow centre.
Flowers occur in clusters.
The rounded leaf tip is especially useful because it helps distinguish this plant from Plumeria pudica.
Flowers and season
The flowers are white with a yellow centre and are usually fragrant.
In warm climates, it can flower for long periods of the year.
Fruit
It can produce long, narrow paired seed pods. These eventually split and release seeds that can be carried by wind.
Origin
Despite the name Singapore Frangipani, it is not originally from Singapore. Its natural range includes southeastern Mexico, Honduras and parts of the Caribbean.
Uses
Mostly grown for decoration in:
gardens
parks
campuses
roadsides
courtyards
Safety
It produces milky latex when damaged, which can irritate the skin.
Interesting fact
It belongs to the same plant family as Oleander, the Apocynaceae family.
Common name: Gulmohar / Flame Tree / Royal Poinciana
Scientific name: Delonix regia
Family: Fabaceae
Characteristics for identification
Very fine, feathery leaves.
Leaves are bipinnate, meaning they are divided twice.
Many tiny leaflets are arranged along smaller branches.
Mature trees can have a broad, spreading crown.
Large red or orange-red flowers appear when the tree blooms.
Long, flat, woody seed pods develop after flowering.
Flowers
The flowers are usually scarlet, crimson or orange-red.
One of the five petals is different from the other four. It often has yellow or white markings with red streaks.
Flowering season
In India, flowering is generally associated with the warmer months and summer, although the exact timing varies.
Fruit
After flowering, it produces very large, flat woody pods. They can reach around 30–60 cm and turn dark brown or almost black when mature.
Uses
It is commonly planted for:
shade
roads
gardens
parks
avenues
landscaping
Origin
Gulmohar is native to Madagascar.
Interesting facts
The leaves look almost like delicate green feathers.
Also, the crown of a mature Gulmohar can become very wide, sometimes wider than the tree is tall.
One important identification caution: Copperpod can have similar feathery leaves, so the red/orange flowers or large pods help confirm Gulmohar.
Common name: Porcupine Flower / Vajradanti
Scientific name: Barleria prionitis L.
Family: Acanthaceae
Characteristics for identification
Small, bushy shrub.
Opposite green leaves.
Yellow or orange-yellow tubular flowers.
Flowers occur near the ends of branches.
Sharp spines occur around the leaf axils.
Those spines are one of the best identification clues.
Flowering season
Flowering can vary with climate. It is often associated with the autumn or cooler months, but it can flower at other times too.
Fruit
It produces a small capsule containing seeds.
Uses and traditional medicine
It is used as an ornamental plant.

The plant is also known as Vajradanti and has a history of traditional medicinal use, including traditional remedies involving tooth and other health problems. These traditional uses should not be presented as proven cures.
Interesting fact
The name Porcupine Flower comes from the sharp spines around the leaves. The plant can look a little prickly like a porcupine.
A possible look-alike is yellow Ixora, but Ixora usually has denser rounded flower clusters, while Barleria prionitis has more spike-like clusters and tubular flowers.
Common name: Karonda / Bengal Currant / Lasoda
Scientific name: Carissa carandas L.
Family: Apocynaceae
Characteristics for identification
Evergreen shrub or small tree.
Dense, bushy growth.
Glossy, leathery leaves.
Leaves occur opposite each other.
Woody, branching stems.
Sharp spines at the branches or nodes.
The photograph does not show the spines clearly, so the identification was recorded as moderate rather than certain.
Flowers
Karonda produces small, white, fragrant flowers, usually in clusters. In India, flowering is commonly reported around March to June, although this varies.
Fruit
The fruits are small and round or oval.
They change colour as they ripen:
green → red → purple/black
The ripe fruit is edible and has a sour or acidic taste.
It is used for:
pickles
chutneys
jams
jellies
syrups
Uses
Because of its sharp spines and dense growth, it can also be used as a living fence or protective hedge.
Medicinal use
Traditional medicinal uses have been reported, but these should not be presented as proven medical treatments.
Interesting fact
If you see green, red and dark-purple fruits on the same plant, they can simply be fruits at different stages of ripening.
Common name: Copperleaf / Firestorm / Dwarf Acalypha
Scientific name: Acalypha godseffiana 'Heterophylla'
Family: Euphorbiaceae
Characteristics for identification
Narrow green leaves.
Leaves have strongly wavy or ruffled edges.
The edges have a noticeable pink or reddish colour.
Leaves grow alternately along woody stems.
Bushy shrub.
The pink, wavy leaf margin is the best clue.
Flowers
The flowers are small and not very noticeable. They appear in spikes near the leaf axils.
The plant is mainly grown for its foliage rather than its flowers.
Uses
Mostly used as an ornamental plant in:
gardens
parks
borders
hedges
landscaped campuses
Interesting fact
The pink edge of the leaves is not damage or dying tissue. It is part of the plant's natural colouring, and stronger light can make the colours more noticeable.
Medicinal / safety
I would not add medicinal claims for this plant. It is mainly an ornamental foliage plant and should not be treated as food or a home remedy.
Likely common name: Indian Bay Leaf / Indonesian Bay Leaf / Salam
Likely scientific name: Syzygium polyanthum (Wight) Walp.
Family: Myrtaceae
Important identification note
This one is not fully confirmed.

The three photographs appear to show the same plant, and they strongly fit the Syzygium genus, but Syzygium polyanthum is only a moderate-confidence identification because several Syzygium species look similar.
Characteristics
Dense evergreen foliage.
Simple, glossy leaves.
Leaves are narrow and pointed.
Leaves grow in opposite pairs.
Woody branching stems.
Small cream-white flowers in clusters.
Flowers and fruit
The flowers are small, cream-white and have many stamens, giving them a fluffy appearance.
If it is S. polyanthum, it produces small fleshy berries that can change from green to red and then purplish-black.
Uses
This is the interesting part.
The leaves are known as Salam leaves or Indonesian bay leaves and are used as a flavouring herb in Southeast Asian cooking. They can be used fresh or dried.
Flowering season
Flowering and fruiting can occur through much of the year in suitable tropical conditions.
Traditional uses
Traditional medicinal uses of the leaves, bark and roots have been reported, but they should not be presented as proven medical treatments.
Important point for our final list
I would currently write:
Syzygium sp. — likely Syzygium polyanthum, not yet confirmed.
A close-up of the flowers, underside of a leaf, fruit, and leaf attachment would help confirm it.
Common name: Sessile Joyweed / Dwarf Copperleaf
Scientific name: Alternanthera sessilis
Family: Amaranthaceae
Characteristics
Small, low-growing herb.
Stems can spread along the ground.
Leaves occur in opposite pairs.
Leaves are simple, smooth-edged and somewhat fleshy.
Small white or pale flowers occur in compact round clusters where the leaves meet the stem.
Flowering season
It can flower through much of the year, especially in warm and moist conditions.
Uses
This is an interesting plant because the young leaves and shoots can be eaten as a leafy vegetable in parts of Asia.
It naturally grows in moist places such as:
ponds
canals
marshy ground
irrigated fields
Traditional medicinal use
It has a history of traditional medicinal use, but I would keep that statement general rather than saying it cures specific diseases.
Interesting fact
The plant can produce roots from its stem nodes. In simple words, when a creeping stem touches moist soil, roots can grow from the places where the leaves arise. This helps the plant spread.
Common name: Custard Apple / Sugar Apple / Sweetsop / Sitaphal / Sharifa
Scientific name: Annona squamosa L.
Family: Annonaceae
Characteristics
Small tree or large shrub.
Smooth green leaves.
Leaves are oval to lance-shaped.
Flowers are small and greenish.
Fruit is round or slightly heart-shaped with many raised sections.
Ripe fruit has soft, creamy-white pulp.
Seeds are dark brown or black.
Fruit
This is the main reason people grow it.
The ripe pulp is sweet and creamy and can be eaten fresh. It is also used in:
milkshakes
ice cream
desserts
other fruit products
Flowering season
It generally flowers in spring and early summer, with fruits developing and ripening later in the year. The exact timing varies by region.
Important warning
The seeds should not be eaten. They can be toxic and irritating, especially if seed material gets into the eyes.
Medicinal use
Different parts have been used traditionally, but I would not turn those traditional uses into claims that the plant cures diseases.
Interesting fact
The bumps or “scales” on the outside of the fruit are actually individual sections of the fruit that have grown together.
Common name: Fukien Tea / Philippine Tea / Carmona
Scientific name: Ehretia microphylla Lam.
Older/common synonym: Carmona retusa
Family: Boraginaceae
Characteristics
Dense, heavily branched shrub.
Small, thick, glossy leaves.
Leaves have a slightly wrinkled or bumpy surface.
Woody branches.
Compact growth.
Flowers
The flowers are small and white, usually appearing singly or in small clusters near the leaf axils.
An Indian botanical record gives flowering and fruiting around July to March, although this can vary.
Fruit
The plant produces small round fruits that become bright red when mature.
Seeing white flowers together with red berries would make the identification much stronger.
Uses
It is mainly grown as an ornamental shrub and is particularly popular as a bonsai plant.
Its small leaves and woody branches make it easy to train into a miniature tree.
Medicinal use
Traditional medicinal uses are reported, but they are not something I would emphasize without stronger evidence.
Interesting fact
Even though it is naturally a shrub, it can be trained to look like a tiny tree in bonsai form.
Common name: Subabul / Subabool / Lead Tree / Leucaena / Wild Tamarind
Scientific name: Leucaena leucocephala
Family: Fabaceae
Characteristics
Small to medium tree or shrub.
Very fine, feathery leaves.
Leaves are bipinnate.
Tiny leaflets give the leaves a fern-like appearance.
Small white or cream flower heads are round.
Long, flat seed pods develop later.
Flowers and season
The flowers occur in round, ball-like heads and are usually white or cream.
It can flower for much of the year, especially in warm climates.
Fruit
The pods are long, flat and straight. They are green when young and brown when mature.
Uses
Subabul has many practical uses:
animal fodder
green manure
fuel
charcoal
soil protection and cover crops
Important caution
Subabul contains a natural compound called mimosine. Too much of it can cause health problems in livestock, so its use as animal feed needs to be controlled.
It can also become invasive in some places because it grows quickly and produces many seeds.
Interesting facts
Its leaves can fold in response to things such as heat, cold or lack of water.
The leaves are so finely divided that they can look almost like tiny ferns.
Common name: Indian Cherry / Lasora / Lasoda / Bhokar / Gonda
Scientific name: Cordia dichotoma G.Forst.
Family: Boraginaceae
Characteristics
Small to medium woody tree or shrub.
Long, drooping branches.
Broad green leaves.
Leaves are oval to elliptical.
Margins can be slightly wavy.
Veins are quite visible.
Flowers
The flowers are small, white and fragrant.
One interesting feature is that the flowers can open at night.
Flowering is generally around spring and early summer.
Fruit
The fruit is one of the best ways to confirm the plant.
The fruits can be round or oval and may become yellowish, pinkish or pale when ripe. They contain a sticky, jelly-like pulp.
The fruit is edible and is used in some parts of India for pickles and other traditional foods.
Medicinal use
Traditional medicinal uses have been reported, but these should not be presented as proven medical treatments.
Interesting fact
The combination of fragrant flowers that can open at night and sticky fruit makes this plant quite interesting.
Common name: Japanese Pittosporum / Japanese Mock Orange / Japanese Cheesewood / Tobira
Scientific name: Pittosporum tobira
Family: Pittosporaceae
Characteristics
Evergreen shrub or small tree.
Thick, leathery leaves.
Leaves are glossy and dark green.
Leaves are oval or spoon-shaped.
Leaves are gathered in dense clusters at the ends of branches.
The cluster of thick leaves at the branch tips is one of the best clues.
Flowers and season
The flowers are small, white and five-petalled. They later become creamy or yellowish.
They are strongly fragrant, with a smell often compared to orange blossom.
Flowering is generally in spring, around March to May depending on climate.
Fruit
After flowering, it develops a woody capsule.
When the capsule opens, it reveals bright red, sticky seeds.
Uses
It is mainly used as an ornamental shrub for:
hedges
borders
privacy screens
gardens
landscaping
It tolerates pruning well and can also handle some salt, wind and drought once established.
Interesting facts
Its flowers smell similar to orange blossom, even though it is not an orange tree.
Also, its seeds are sticky. This is connected to the meaning behind the name Pittosporum
Common name: Areca Palm / Golden Cane Palm / Butterfly Palm
Scientific name: Chrysalidocarpus lutescens H.Wendl.
Older/common scientific name: Dypsis lutescens
Family: Arecaceae
Characteristics
Several slender stems grow together from the base.
Long, feather-like leaves.
Many narrow leaflets along each leaf stalk.
Dense, clumping appearance.
Stems can have a yellowish or golden colour.
Flowers and fruit
The flowers are small and yellowish and occur in branching clusters among the leaves.
After flowering, it can produce small oval fruits that become yellowish or orange as they mature.
Flowering season
Flowering depends greatly on climate and growing conditions, so a strict month is not useful. Warm conditions encourage flowering.
Uses
It is mainly an ornamental palm used in:
gardens
courtyards
parks
building entrances
landscaping
suitable indoor spaces
Its dense growth can also act as a natural screen.
Origin
It is originally from Madagascar.
Interesting facts
Despite being called an “Areca Palm,” its currently accepted scientific name is Chrysalidocarpus lutescens.
Also, it is not a single-trunk palm. Several stems grow together from the base, which gives it its bushy look.
Common name: Creeping Fig / Climbing Fig / Creeping Ficus
Scientific name: Ficus pumila L.
Family: Moraceae
Characteristics
Evergreen woody climber.
Glossy green leaves.
Leaves are simple and usually oval to somewhat heart-shaped.
It produces aerial rootlets that attach to walls, trees and other surfaces.
The really interesting feature
Creeping Fig can have two very different kinds of leaves on the same plant.
When it is young and climbing, the leaves are small.
Later, mature fruiting branches can develop much larger and thicker leaves.
This difference between leaf forms is called heterophylly.
Flowers and fruit
The flowers are not normally visible because they are inside the structure we call the fig.
The plant can produce pear-shaped figs that start green and can become reddish or dark purple.
Uses
It is grown to cover:
walls
fences
trellises
structures
ground areas
Its aerial roots grip surfaces strongly, although this can sometimes make the plant difficult to remove.
Interesting facts
It doesn't need to wrap around a support like a normal vine. Its aerial roots stick to the surface.
Also, what we call the “fig” is actually a special structure containing the flowers inside it.
Common name: Chinese Hibiscus / Shoe Flower / Hibiscus
Scientific name: Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis
Family: Malvaceae
Characteristics
Large yellow flower.
Flower is double or semi-double.
Glossy green leaves.
Leaves have toothed edges.
Woody branching shrub.
The exact yellow cultivar cannot be identified from the photograph alone because there are many similar cultivated varieties.
Flowers
The yellow flower is the main attraction.
In a normal single hibiscus, there is a long central staminal column. In double flowers, some of the stamens can become extra petals, making the flower look fuller.
Flowering season
In warm tropical climates, it can flower repeatedly through much of the year.
Uses
It is mainly ornamental and is used in:
gardens
school grounds
hedges
containers
courtyards
landscaping
Medicinal significance
Hibiscus has a long history of traditional uses, but it is better not to tell students that the plant is a medicine or that it cures diseases.
Interesting facts
There are many cultivated Hibiscus varieties with different colours and flower shapes.
Also, Hibiscus belongs to the Malvaceae family, the same family that includes cotton and okra.
Note: This is essentially the same type of plant as Plant 23, so if the goal is 45 different plants, I would combine them rather than count both.
Common name: Jungle Flame / Jungle Geranium / Flame of the Woods / Red Ixora / Ixora
Scientific name: Ixora coccinea L.
Family: Rubiaceae
Characteristics
Evergreen flowering shrub.
Glossy, dark-green leaves.
Leaves are opposite.
Young stems can have a reddish colour.
Dense clusters of bright tubular flowers.
Flowers usually have four petals.
Flowers
The flowers are usually bright red or scarlet and are long and tubular.
They can also occur in:
pink
orange
yellow
white
What looks like one big flower is actually a cluster of many small individual flowers.
Flowering season
It mainly flowers in summer, but in warm tropical places it can bloom almost throughout the year.
Fruit
The fruit is a small round drupe. It starts green and can become dark purple or almost black when ripe.
Uses
Mostly grown as an ornamental plant for:
gardens
flower beds
borders
hedges
landscaping
Its dense growth also makes it useful as a screen.
Medicinal significance

Ixora has a history of traditional medicinal use, and different parts have been studied for several possible biological effects. However, this should not be presented as proof that Ixora cures diseases.
Interesting facts
Ixora belongs to the same botanical family as coffee.
Also, its large colourful flower cluster is actually made up of many individual flowers.
Common name: Gardenia / Cape Jasmine / Cape Jessamine
Scientific name: Gardenia jasminoides J.Ellis
Family: Rubiaceae
Characteristics
Evergreen shrub.
Very glossy, dark-green leaves.
Leaves are thick and leathery.
Prominent veins.
White, waxy-looking flowers.
Strong, sweet fragrance.
Long flower buds can have a twisted or spiral appearance.
Flowers and flowering season
The flowers are white to creamy white and are very strongly scented.
In warmer climates, Gardenia can flower for much of the year. In cooler places, flowering is more concentrated around late spring and summer.
Fruit
After flowering, it produces a fleshy fruit that becomes yellow-orange or reddish-orange as it matures.
The fruit contains natural compounds such as crocin and geniposide.
One especially interesting use is that Gardenia fruit has traditionally been used as a natural yellow colouring.
Uses
Gardenia is mainly grown as an ornamental plant, especially near:
walkways
doors
windows
gardens
flower beds
places where people can enjoy its fragrance
Its fruit has also been used as a natural yellow pigment in food, textiles and other applications.
Medicinal significance / caution
Gardenia fruit has a long history in traditional Chinese medicine, and researchers have studied some of its compounds.
However, traditional use does not automatically mean it is safe to use as medicine. Some medicinal preparations can have risks, particularly with inappropriate or prolonged use.
Interesting facts
Gardenia, Ixora and coffee all belong to the Rubiaceae family.
And perhaps the nicest fact for a student: the fruit can be used to make natural yellow colouring
Common name: Jackfruit / Kathal
Scientific name: Artocarpus heterophyllus
Family: Moraceae
Characteristics for identification:
A large evergreen tree with a thick trunk and broad, dense foliage.
Leaves are thick, glossy and dark green.
Young leaves can sometimes have a slightly lobed shape, while mature leaves are usually oval and smooth.
The tree produces very large fruits directly from the trunk and large branches, which is one of its easiest features to notice.
The fruit has a rough green or yellowish-green skin covered with small, hard, pointed bumps.
The tree contains a sticky white latex, especially when a fruit or branch is cut.

Uses: The ripe fruit is eaten fresh because the yellow flesh is sweet and fragrant. Unripe jackfruit is commonly cooked as a vegetable, especially in Indian cooking. The seeds can also be boiled, roasted or cooked.
Origin: Jackfruit is believed to have originated in the rainforests of the Western Ghats of India. It is now grown in many tropical parts of the world.
Flowering season and fruits:
Jackfruit has separate male and female flower clusters on the same tree. The flowers are small and are produced on the trunk and branches.

The fruits are usually seen during the warmer and monsoon months, although the exact fruiting season can change according to the region and climate. Jackfruit can produce fruits directly from the trunk, which is quite unusual for a large tree.
The jackfruit is considered the largest tree-borne fruit in the world. Large fruits can become extremely heavy, and a single fruit can contain many seeds.
Fun fact: Unlike most fruits that hang from small branches, jackfruit can grow straight out of the trunk. This type of fruiting is called cauliflory.
Common name: Mango / Aam
Scientific name: Mangifera indica
Family: Anacardiaceae
Characteristics for identification:
A large evergreen tree with a thick trunk and a broad, rounded crown.
Leaves are long, narrow, leathery and glossy.
New leaves are often copper, reddish or light green before becoming dark green.
Leaves usually grow in clusters near the ends of branches.
The tree has rough, greyish-brown bark as it becomes older.
Mango fruits are usually oval or slightly kidney-shaped, although their shape and colour can vary a lot between varieties.

Uses: Mango is mainly grown for its fruit. Raw mangoes are used for pickles, chutneys and other foods, while ripe mangoes are eaten fresh or used to make juice, shakes and desserts. Mango leaves are also used for decoration during some Indian festivals and ceremonies.
Origin: Mango is native to South Asia, particularly the Indian subcontinent and nearby regions. India has a very long history of growing and cultivating mangoes.
Flowering season and fruits:
In many parts of India, mango trees produce their flowers mainly around January to March. The flowers are very small and grow together in large branched clusters called panicles.
The fruits generally mature around May to July, but the exact time depends on the variety and location.
Mango trees can become very large and live for many years.
Fun fact: Mango is the national fruit of India. Also, the new leaves of a mango tree can look completely different from the older dark-green leaves because they often start out copper-coloured.
Common name: Jamun / Indian blackberry / Java plum / Black plum
Scientific name: Syzygium cumini
Family: Myrtaceae
Characteristics for identification:
A medium to large evergreen tree with a dense crown.
Leaves are thick, smooth and glossy.
The leaves are usually oval to slightly elongated and have a noticeable smell when crushed.
The bark is greyish-brown and becomes rougher as the tree gets older.
The fruits are small and oval or elongated.
They start green and become deep purple to almost black when ripe.
Uses: The ripe fruit is eaten fresh and has a sweet but slightly astringent taste. It can also be used to make juice, jam, jelly, squash and other products.
Origin: Jamun is native to the Indian subcontinent and surrounding parts of South Asia. It is now widely grown in different parts of India.
Flowering season and fruits:
Jamun usually flowers before the fruiting season. The fruit develops during the warmer months and becomes dark purple or almost black when ripe.
The tree prefers relatively dry weather during flowering and fruit setting, while some rainfall later helps the fruits develop properly.
Medicinal and nutritional information:

Jamun fruits contain minerals, sugars, iron and other nutrients. Jamun seeds and other parts of the plant have also been used traditionally in Indian systems of medicine. Research has investigated several possible biological effects of jamun, but these should not be taken as a replacement for medical treatment.
Fun fact: The ripe fruit can stain your tongue and lips purple. The deep colour comes from natural pigments called anthocyanins.
Location note: The blue jamun near the guesthouse, where the pots have been arranged, can be recorded as this plant.
Common name: Papaya / Papita
Scientific name: Carica papaya
Family: Caricaceae
Characteristics for identification:
Papaya is a small, fast-growing plant with a soft, usually unbranched trunk.
The trunk is hollow and has marks left behind by old leaves.
Large leaves grow mainly near the top of the plant.
The leaves are deeply divided and look somewhat like the fingers of a hand.
Papaya fruits are large, smooth and usually green when unripe.
As they ripen, they usually turn yellow or orange.
The inside contains orange or yellow flesh and many small black seeds.
Uses: Ripe papaya is eaten fresh and is also used in juices, salads and desserts. Green papaya can be cooked as a vegetable.
Papaya also contains an enzyme called papain, which is used in some food and industrial applications.
Origin: Papaya originally came from tropical America but is now grown widely in tropical and subtropical countries, including India.
Flowering season and fruits:

Papaya can flower and produce fruits relatively quickly compared with many fruit trees. Under suitable conditions, plants can start producing fruit around 8–10 months after planting and can continue producing for around 2–3 years.
The flowers can be male, female or bisexual depending on the type of papaya plant. This means that not every papaya plant produces fruit in exactly the same way.
Important note: The milky sap from an unripe papaya can irritate the skin in some people. The seeds are generally not eaten in the same way as the fruit flesh.
Fun fact: Papaya is sometimes called a tree, but botanically it is more like a giant herb because its stem is soft and does not form normal woody branches like a typical tree.

header: Plant 46 – Banana [ two types/species are there]
paragraphs: Common name: Banana / Kela
Scientific name: Musa spp.
Family: Musaceae
Characteristics for identification:
Banana has very large, long leaves that grow from the centre of the plant.
The leaves are broad and soft and can easily tear in strong wind.
What looks like a trunk is actually a pseudostem, made from tightly packed leaf bases.
Banana plants grow quickly and can form a large group of plants around the original plant.
The flower develops from the centre and eventually hangs downward.
Banana fruits grow together in bunches, sometimes with many individual bananas.

Uses: Ripe bananas are eaten fresh and are also used in shakes, desserts and many cooked foods. Green bananas can be cooked as a vegetable. Banana flowers are also eaten in some parts of India. The leaves are traditionally used as plates or for serving food in several regions.
Origin: Bananas have a long history of cultivation in South and Southeast Asia. Today they are grown throughout tropical and subtropical regions.
Flowering season and fruits:
Banana does not have one fixed flowering season in the same way as many seasonal trees. In suitable warm conditions, a plant can produce its flower after reaching the right stage of growth.

The flower, called the banana inflorescence, comes out from the centre of the pseudostem. The female flowers develop into the bananas. In many edible varieties, the fruits develop without needing pollination and are usually seedless.

Fun fact: A banana plant is not technically a tree. It is one of the world's largest flowering herbaceous plants. Also, what we commonly call the banana "trunk" is actually made from tightly wrapped leaf sheaths.

Another interesting point: After one banana plant produces its bunch, that particular pseudostem does not keep producing forever. New shoots, called suckers, grow from the base and can produce the next crop.
